As "I beseech you" (a distinct Greek verb, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2Co 10:2</reference>) for my sake.<div eID="gen34587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the meekness and gentleness of Christ--</hi>He mentions these graces of Christ especially (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.35">Psa 18:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>), as on account of his imitation of them in particular he was despised [Grotius]. He entreats them by these, in order to show that though he must have recourse to more severe measures, he is naturally inclined to gentle ones after Christ's example [Menochius]. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 10 2Co 10:1-18 . He Vindicates His Apostolic Authority against Those Who Depreciated Him for His Personal Appearance. He Will Make His Power Felt When He Comes. He Boasts Not, as They, Beyond His Measure. 1. I Paul myself-- no longer "we," "us," "our" ( 2Co 9:11 ): I who am represented by depreciators as "base," I, the same Paul, of my own accord "beseech you"; or rather "entreat," "exhort" you for your sake. As "I beseech you" (a distinct Greek verb, 2Co 10:2 ) for my sake. by the meekness and gentleness of Christ-- He mentions these graces of Christ especially ( Psa 18:35 ; Mt 11:29 ), as on account of his imitation of them in particular he was despised [Grotius]. He entreats them by these, in order to show that though he must have recourse to more severe measures, he is naturally inclined to gentle ones after Christ's example [Menochius]. "Meekness" is more in the mind internally; "gentleness" in the external behavior, and in relation to others; for instance, the condescending yieldingness of a superior to an inferior, the former not insisting on his strict rights [Trench]. Bengel explains it, "By the meekness and gentleness derived by me from Christ," not from my own nature: he objects to understanding it of Christ's meekness and gentleness, since nowhere else is "gentleness" attributed to Him. But though the exact Greek word is not applied to Him, the idea expressed by it is (compare Is 40:11 ; Mt 12:19 , 20 ). in presence-- in personal appearance when present with you. base-- Greek, "lowly"; timid, humbly diffident: opposed to "bold." "Am" stands here by ironical concession for "am reputed to be" (compare 2Co 10:10 ).

entries.content_plain: 2. I beseech you-- Intimating that, as he can beseech in letters, so he can be severe in their presence. that I may not be-- that I may not have to be bold, &c. with that confidence-- that authoritative sternness. I think-- I am minded to be. as if we walked according to the flesh-- His Corinthian detractors judged of him by themselves, as if he were influenced by fleshly motives, the desire of favor or fear of giving offense, so as not to exercise his authority when present.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17341"/><div sID="gen34596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17341"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>Reason why they should regard him "beseeching" them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2Co 10:2</reference>) not to oblige him to have recourse to "bold" and stern exercise of authority. "We walk IN the flesh," and so in weakness: but not "ACCORDING TO the flesh" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2Co 10:2</reference>). Moreover, though we WALK in it, we do not WAR according to it. A double contrast or antithesis. "They who accuse us of walking after the flesh, shall find [to their cost] that we do not war after the flesh; therefore compel us not to use our weapons" [Alford]. <div eID="gen34596" type="x-p"/>

A confutation of those who try to propagate their creed by force and persecution (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.9.54-Luke.9.56">Lu 9:54-56</reference>).<div eID="gen34597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weapons--</hi>for punishing offending members (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.6">2Co 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.21">1Co 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.13">13</reference>); boldness of speech, ecclesiastical discipline (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.8">2Co 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.10">2Co 13:10</reference>), the power of the word, and of the sacraments, the various extraordinary gifts of the Spirit.<div eID="gen34598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carnal--</hi>Translate, "fleshly," to preserve the allusion to <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2Co 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.3">3</reference>.<div eID="gen34599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty through God--</hi>Greek, "mighty to God," that is, mighty before God: not humanly, but divinely powerful. The power is not ours, but God's. Compare "fair to God," that is, divinely fair (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.20">Ac 7:20</reference>, Margin). Also above (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2Co 2:15</reference>), "unto God a sweet savor." "The efficacy of the Christian religion proves its truth" [Bengel].<div eID="gen34600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pulling down--</hi>As the Greek is the same as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2Co 10:5</reference>, translate, "casting down." Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jr 1:10</reference>: the inspired servants of God inherit the commission of the Old Testament prophets.<div eID="gen34601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strongholds--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.21.22">Pr 21:22</reference>); namely, in which sinners entrench themselves against reproof; all that opposes itself to Christ; the learning, and eloquence, and philosophical subtleties on which the Corinthians prided themselves. So Joshua's trumpet blast was "mighty" under God to overthrow the walls of Jericho. <div eID="gen34602" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17343"/><div sID="gen34603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17343"/><hi type="bold">5. imaginations--</hi>rather, "reasonings." Whereas "thought" expresses men's own purpose and determination of living after their own pleasure [Tittmann].<div eID="gen34603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high thing--</hi>So it ought to be translated (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">Ro 8:39</reference>). A distinct Greek word from that in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>, "height," and <reference osisRef="Rev.21.16">Re 21:16</reference>, which belongs to God and heaven from whence we receive nothing hurtful. But "high thing" is not so much "height" as something made high, and belongs to those regions of air where the powers of darkness ::exalt themselves" against Christ and us (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exalteth itself--</hi><reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference> supports English Version rather than the translation of Ellicott, &c., "is lifted up." Such were the high towers of Judaic self-righteousness, philosophic speculations, and rhetorical sophistries, the "knowledge" so much prized by many (opposed to "the knowledge of God"), which endangered a section of the Corinthian Church.<div eID="gen34605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the knowledge of God--</hi>True knowledge makes men humble. Where there is exaltation of self, there knowledge of God is wanting [Bengel]. Arrange the words following thus: "Bringing every thought (that is, intent of the mind or will) into captivity to the obedience of Christ," that is, to obey Christ. The three steps of the apostle's spiritual warfare are: (1) It demolishes what is opposed to Christ; (2) It leads captive; (3) It brings into obedience to Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.5">Ro 1:5</reference>; 16:26). The "reasonings" (English Version, "imaginations") are utterly "cast down." The "mental intents" (English Version, "thoughts") are taken willing captives, and tender the voluntary obedience of faith to Christ the Conqueror. <div eID="gen34606" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17344"/><div sID="gen34607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17344"/>6. Translate, "Having ourselves (that is, being) in readiness to exact punishment for all disobedience," &c. We have this in store for the disobedient: it will be brought into action in due time.<div eID="gen34607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when your obedience, &c.--</hi>He charitably assumes that most of the Corinthian Church will act obediently; therefore he says "YOUR obedience." But perhaps some will act otherwise; in order, therefore, to give all an opportunity of joining the obedient, he will not prematurely exact punishment, but wait until the full number of those gathered out to Christ has been "completed," and the remainder have been proved incorrigible. He had acted already so at Corinth (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.6-Acts.18.11">Ac 18:6-11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.34">Ex 32:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.28-Matt.13.30">Mt 13:28-30</reference>). <div eID="gen34608" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17345"/><div sID="gen34609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17345"/>7. Do ye regard mere outward appearance (mere external recommendations, personal appearance, voice, manner, oratory of teachers present face to face, such as they admired in the false teachers to the disparagement of Paul, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12">2Co 5:12</reference>)? Even in outward bearing when I shall be present with you (in contrast to "by letters," <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.9">2Co 10:9</reference>) I will show that I am more really armed with the authority of Christ, than those who arrogate to themselves the title of being peculiarly "Christ's" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">1Co 1:12</reference>). A Jewish emissary seems to have led this party.<div eID="gen34609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let him of himself think this again--</hi>He may "of himself," without needing to be taught it in a more severe manner, by "thinking again," arrive at "this" conclusion, "that even as," &c. Paul modestly demands for himself only an equal place with those whom he had begotten in the Gospel [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34610" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17346"/><div sID="gen34611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17346"/>8. "For even if I were to boast somewhat more exceedingly (than I do, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.3-2Cor.10.6">2Co 10:3-6</reference>) of our (apostolic) authority (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.6">2Co 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.10">2Co 13:10</reference>) ... I should not be put to shame (by the fact; as I should be if my authority proved to be without foundation: my threats of punishment not being carried into effect)."<div eID="gen34611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for edification ... not for ... destruction--</hi>Greek, "for building up ... not for ... CASTING DOWN" (the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2Co 10:5</reference>): the image of a building as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">5</reference>. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17350"/><div sID="gen34619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17350"/>12. "We do not presume (irony) to judge ourselves among, or in comparison with, some of them that commend themselves." The charge falsely brought against him of commending himself (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12">5:12</reference>), really holds good of the false teachers. The phrase, "judge ourselves of the number," is drawn from the testing of athletes and senators, the "approved" being set down on the roll [Wahl].<div eID="gen34619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">measuring themselves by themselves--</hi>"among themselves": to correspond to the previous verb, "judge ourselves among them." Instead of measuring themselves by the public standard, they measure themselves by one made by themselves: they do not compare themselves with others who excel them, but with those like themselves: hence their high self-esteem. The one-eyed is easily king among the blind.<div eID="gen34620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are not wise--</hi>with all their boasted "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19-1Cor.1.26">1Co 1:19-26</reference>), they are anything but "wise." <div eID="gen34621" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17351"/><div sID="gen34622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17351"/><hi type="bold">13. not boast ... without ... measure--</hi>Greek, "to unmeasured bounds." There is no limit to a man's high opinion of himself, so long as he measures himself by himself (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.13">2Co 10:13</reference>) and his fellows, and does not compare himself with his superiors. It marks the personal character of this Epistle that the word "boast" occurs twenty-nine times in it, and only twenty-six times in all the other Epistles put together. Undeterred by the charge of vanity, he felt he must vindicate his apostolic authority by facts [Conybeare and Howson]. It would be to "boast of things without our measure," were we to boast of conversions made by "other men's labors" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.15">2Co 10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen34622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">distributed--</hi>apportioned [Alford].<div eID="gen34623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a measure--</hi>as a measure [Alford].<div eID="gen34624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to reach--</hi>"that we should reach as far as even to you": not that he meant to go no further (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.16">2Co 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.20-Rom.15.24">Ro 15:20-24</reference>). Paul's "measure" is the apportionment of his sphere of Gospel labors ruled for him by God. A "rule" among the so-called "apostolic canons" subsequently was, that no bishop should appoint ministers beyond his own limits. At Corinth no minister ought to have been received without Paul's sanction, as Corinth was apportioned to him by God as his apostolic sphere. The Epistle here incidentally, and therefore undesignedly, confirms the independent history, the Acts, which represents Corinth as the extreme limit as yet of his preaching, at which he had stopped, after he had from Philippi passed southward successively through Amphipolis, Apollonia, Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens [Paley, Horæ Paulinæ]. <div eID="gen34625" type="x-p"/>
